vignette:
Sameer, a 58-year-old product manager, presented as a man holding himself together with immense effort. His posture was rigid, his gaze constantly scanning the room, and he spoke in quiet, clipped sentences. The events that shattered his world had occurred eight months prior, during a business trip to a country where he was a visible minority. Mistaken for a political dissident, he was detained and held for three days. The experience was a blur of disorientation and terror: the constant, incomprehensible chatter of his captors in a language he couldn't place, the suffocating hood that left him dizzy and nauseous, and the recurring wail of sirens from the street outside, each blast a fresh wave of fear. He remembers the rough fabric of a uniform, the cold metal of a weapon pressed against his neck, and the profound, chilling certainty that he would die there.

Since his release and return home, Sameer has found that the interrogation room has, in a sense, come with him. He has come to believe that the world is fundamentally a dangerous place and that people, by their nature, cannot be trusted. This deep-seated conviction that he is unsafe fuels a state of relentless hypervigilance. He is unable to relax, even in his own home with his wife, Anjali, and startles violently at the slightest unexpected touch. Most nights, he finds himself waking abruptly in the dark, heart pounding, listening for intruders and checking the locks he knows he has already secured. In this state of constant, exhausting tension, his sensitivity to perceived threats has sharpened, and even the distant sound of an ambulance siren now feels like a personal, imminent danger closing in.

This pervasive sense of threat has dictated the radical reshaping of his life. Because he feels perpetually unsafe, Sameer has adopted a series of rigid strategies to manage the perceived danger. Having concluded that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place, these behaviours felt less like a choice and more like a logical, necessary shield against inevitable harm. He has begun to constantly monitor his own body, scanning for any sign of injury or a recurrence of the dizzying disorientation he felt while captive. This relentless internal focus has, in turn, made him exquisitely sensitive to the very sensations he fears; the slightest feeling of lightheadedness from standing up too quickly now registers as a terrifying trigger, plunging him back into the memory of the hood. He also meticulously avoids any situation he deems potentially stressful, a category that has expanded to include most of his former life. He changes his route to work to avoid driving past the local police station, the sight of the uniforms too much to bear.

These very strategies, meant to keep him safe, have become a cage. His avoidance of stress led him to step back from a major project at work, an opportunity he had been pursuing for years. Seeing a less-experienced colleague take his place cemented his painful belief that there is something intrinsically wrong with him, that he is fundamentally broken by what happened. This feeling of being flawed only deepens his mistrust of others. He watches his colleagues, certain they are judging his weakness. In this way, his attempts to cope only serve to confirm his deepest fears: that he is damaged beyond repair and that nothing good can happen to him anymore.

The office, once a place of achievement, has become a landscape of triggers. The open-plan design means he is often surrounded by the low hum of conversations, and when a nearby team of developers speaks in a language he doesn't understand, the sound of the incomprehensible chatter is enough to make his palms sweat and his vision tunnel. He will abruptly leave his desk, feigning a phone call, and hide in a bathroom stall until the feeling passes. He has used every excuse to work from home, but he knows his career is stalling. It was after he flinched away from Anjali's gentle touch on his shoulder last week, seeing the deep hurt in her eyes, that he finally made this appointment. He is terrified that he is permanently broken, but a small, desperate part of him hopes he can one day feel safe in his own home again.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not state that the patient's negative beliefs (e.g., 'the world is dangerous', 'I am broken') directly lead to his maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, monitoring).

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not state that the patient's negative beliefs (e.g., 'the world is dangerous', 'I am broken') directly lead to his maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, monitoring).
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
